title: State Schemas & Reducers
objective: After this lesson you will be able to design state schemas (channels with types, defaults, reducers), predict merge behavior for concurrent and repeated updates, and keep state minimal, typed, and bounded.
why: Shared mutable state is where agent bugs breed: two nodes overwriting each other's messages, unbounded histories exploding checkpoints, untyped blobs failing downstream. LangGraph's answer — channels with reducers — makes merging explicit and order-safe. State design is the highest-leverage agent skill after topology: every downstream bug is a state bug wearing a costume.

blocks.text: Channels: typed slots with merge rules

State is a set of **channels**: each has a type, a default, and a **reducer** — the function merging an update into current value. Overwrite (default: last write wins) suits single-writer slots (decision, draft). Append/concat suits multi-writer streams (messages, logs). The reducer is declared once in the schema — every merge, everywhere, follows it.

blocks.caption: Declare merge semantics once — order-safe updates everywhere

blocks.text: Three state virtues. **Minimal**: every field must be read by some node — dead fields bloat checkpoints and confuse routers. **Typed**: contracts per channel (Ch.3 enforces them) so nodes can't smuggle shapes. **Bounded**: histories summarize (rolling digest node) instead of growing forever — checkpoint size, cost, and attention all scale with state.

blocks.caption: One merge function, per-channel rules — order-safe by construction

blocks.text: Appending every message forever grows checkpoints linearly with conversation length — slower resumes, pricier calls, blurrier attention. The fix is a **summarizer node** on a schedule (every N steps or K tokens): compress history into a rolling digest, keep recent verbatim, archive the rest outside state. Boundedness is designed, never emergent.

blocks.title: Merge by rule
blocks.note: Run it: expect ["hi","update","again"], attempts=3, decision {ok:true}. Then apply the updates in reverse order and confirm identical results — order-independence is the reducer guarantee.

items: Channels carry type + default + reducer; partials merge by rule, not by accident
Overwrite for single-writer slots, append for streams, counters for tallies — declare once
Minimal (read by someone), typed (contracted), bounded (summarized) — state virtues that prevent whole bug classes

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice merger, then re-run with the two updates swapped; confirm identical final state. (b) Design the returns-graph state (ticket, facts, decision, draft, approval, log, attempts): assign each channel overwrite/append/counter with one-line reasons. (c) State the summarization trigger (every N steps or K tokens) and what the digest keeps vs archives.
hints: Order-swap proof first: identical JSON both ways is the reducer guarantee made visible.
ticket/facts/decision/draft/approval: overwrite (single-writer each). log/messages: append. attempts: counter. Reasons name the writer pattern.
Trigger: every 10 steps or 4k tokens (stated policy); digest keeps decisions + open items, archives verbatim chatter outside state with IDs.
exercise.why: Writer-pattern analysis (who writes what, how often) is the state-design method: channel kinds follow from it mechanically. The swap-proof makes order-safety empirical, not theoretical.
exercise.code: // Swap-proof pattern (playground): apply A-then-B vs B-then-A, diff JSON.

quiz.q: Two nodes append to messages concurrently. Safe because…
options: The append reducer makes merge order-independent — concurrent and sequential updates compose identically
quiz.explain: Reducers move merging from timing to math: concat commutes for streams. Order-safety by construction beats coordination.

quiz.q: Checkpoints balloon as conversations grow. Fix?
options: Summarizer node on schedule: rolling digest in state, verbatim archived outside, recent kept — bounded by design
quiz.explain: Unbounded appends scale cost, latency, and blur linearly. Scheduled summarization bounds state while preserving decisions and open loops.

quiz.q: A channel no node reads. Verdict?
options: Dead weight: checkpoint bloat + router confusion — minimality deletes it
quiz.explain: Minimality: every field earned by a reader. Unread state taxes persistence and misleads debuggers — delete on sight.

summary: Channels with reducers make merges order-safe; minimal/typed/bounded keeps state honest and cheap. State design prevents agent bugs at the source.
next: Blackboard designed — now the workers: node functions with contracts, validation boundaries, and failure behavior. Next: nodes that hold their contracts.
